## Where We're Headed

*From naming the problem precisely to a validated set of solutions.*

1. **Why AI is uniquely difficult** — two root sources of difficulty, and four familiar symptoms
2. **Microsoft's 18 guidelines** — evidence-based design guidance, validated across 20 real products
3. **Guidelines for conversational AI** — which of the 18 apply cleanly, and which struggle without a screen
4. **Putting it together** — connecting the challenges to the guidelines that address them

## Why Is Designing for AI Uniquely Difficult? {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

::: {.kicker}
PART ONE
:::

*HCI routinely handles complex technologies. So what actually makes AI different?*

## The Core Question

*Carnegie Mellon researchers put the question bluntly — and took it seriously.*

::: {.callout}
AI systems can make unpredictable errors that damage the user experience and can even cause societal harm. But HCI has always grappled with complex, error-prone technologies. Yang, Steinfeld, Rosé, and Zimmerman ask directly: what actually makes AI different?
:::

**An uncomfortable finding:** you might expect growing interest in AI to mean HCI designers have gotten good at integrating it. Instead, the authors report the opposite — designers largely struggle to envision and prototype AI systems, even when the AI itself is fairly simple.

*Yang, Q., Steinfeld, A., Rosé, C., & Zimmerman, J. (2020). CHI '20.*

## Two Root Sources of Difficulty {background-color="#003B5C"}

*Yang et al.'s framework traces every AI design headache back to just two things.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Capability Uncertainty**

Designers often can't fully know, in advance, what an AI system can and cannot do — its capabilities are probabilistic and shift as the model is retrained.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Output Complexity**

AI outputs range from simple and predictable to adaptive and complex. Some outputs, the authors note, are "quasi-random" and resist abstraction.
:::
:::
:::

## Four Levels of AI Systems

*Yang et al. show that the design challenges you face depend on where a system sits on this spectrum.*

| Level | Description |
|---|---|
| **1 · Simple, Predictable** | Output is a single, deterministic-feeling result — easiest to sketch and prototype by hand. |
| **2 · Probabilistic** | Output involves confidence or uncertainty the interface must represent. |
| **3 · Multiple Outputs** | The system returns a ranked set of options rather than one answer. |
| **4 · Adaptive & Complex** | Behavior changes over time via learning — hardest to prototype or fully specify. |

## Challenge 1 · Opacity of AI Decision-Making

*Users, and often designers, cannot see how the system reached its conclusion.*

::: {.callout}
Many AI models are effectively black boxes: even their own developers may not be able to fully explain a specific output. Amershi et al. found this directly in their user study — one of the strongest complaints across every product tested was that participants simply couldn't tell why the system did what it did.
:::

**In participants' own words:** one tester of an e-commerce recommender wrote that they had "no idea why this is being shown" to them. Another, testing a music app, found no explanation anywhere for why a specific song had been picked.

## Challenge 2 · Miscalibrated Trust {background-color="#003B5C"}

*Trust that doesn't match a system's actual reliability leads to two opposite failure modes.*

John Lee and Katrina See's foundational review defines the problem precisely: trust guides reliance especially when a system's complexity makes complete understanding impractical — which describes almost every modern AI system.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Overtrust → Misuse**

Users rely on the system beyond its actual competence — accepting a wrong answer without question.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**Distrust → Disuse**

Users abandon a genuinely useful capability after a single visible error.
:::
:::
:::

*Lee, J. D., & See, K. A. (2004). Human Factors, 46(1), 50–80.*

## Challenge 3 · Brittleness

*Systems that work well in typical cases can fail sharply, and without warning, outside them.*

**Errors that surprise everyone:** Amershi et al. note that AI-infused systems can violate a core traditional usability principle — consistency. A model may behave differently under slightly different lighting, phrasing, or context that a person would never even notice as "different."

::: {.callout}
Inconsistent, unpredictable behavior confuses users and erodes their confidence, often leading them to abandon the technology altogether — the "distrust → disuse" pattern, but triggered by the system's own fragility.
:::

## Challenge 4 · Explainability {background-color="#7A0A22"}

*Wanting an explanation and getting a useful one are two very different things.*

::: {.callout}
In Amershi et al.'s user study, Guideline 11 ("Make clear why the system did what it did") had one of the highest numbers of violations of all 18 guidelines — despite a large and growing body of academic research on AI explanations.
:::

**Explanation isn't free, either:** explanations can be gamed by adversarial actors, and may matter far less in low-stakes contexts than in high-stakes ones like medical or financial decisions.

## How These Challenges Compound in Conversational AI

*Recall from Week 5: a conversational interface has no screen to fall back on.*

| | |
|---|---|
| **Opacity** | Without a visible history or UI, users can't even see the inputs the system used. |
| **Miscalibrated trust** | Luger & Sellen's "bad PA" finding is a trust-calibration failure. |
| **Brittleness** | A single misheard word can derail an entire exchange, with no undo button. |
| **Explainability** | "Why did you say that?" has no equivalent of a tooltip in a voice-only interface. |

## Microsoft's 18 Guidelines {background-color="#003B5C"}

::: {.kicker}
PART TWO
:::

*Eighteen evidence-based guidelines, distilled from over 150 recommendations and validated across 20 real products.*

## Where the Guidelines Came From

*Amershi, Weld, Vorvoreanu, et al. (2019) — not opinion, but a four-phase research process.*

| Phase | What happened |
|---|---|
| **1** | 168 design recommendations from industry, articles, and papers → consolidated into 20 guidelines. |
| **2** | 11 internal researchers ran a heuristic evaluation across 13 AI products, refining to 18 guidelines. |
| **3** | 49 HCI practitioners tested the 18 guidelines against 20 popular products, logging 785 real examples. |
| **4** | 11 UX experts reviewed the revised wording to confirm clarity. |

*Amershi, S., Weld, D., Vorvoreanu, M., et al. (2019). CHI '19.*

## Four Categories, Eighteen Guidelines {background-color="#BA0C2F"}

*Organized by when, during a user's interaction, each guideline is most likely to apply.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-midnight}
**G1–G2**

**Initially**

Set the right expectations.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**G3–G6**

**During Interaction**

While actively being used.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-field}
**G7–G11**

**When Wrong**

Invoked, corrected, explained.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="25%"}
::: {.tag-cardinal}
**G12–G18**

**Over Time**

As the relationship evolves.
:::
:::
:::

## Initially · G1–G2 {.smaller}

*Setting the stage before the user has done anything at all.*

**G1 — Make clear what the system can do**
Help the user understand what the AI system is capable of doing. *One activity tracker was praised for showing every metric it tracks and explaining how each is measured.*

**G2 — Make clear how well the system can do what it can do**
Help the user understand how often the AI system may make mistakes. *A music app used gentle hedging language like "we think you'll like" to signal its suggestions weren't certain.*

## During Interaction · G3–G6 {.smaller}

*Guidance for the system while it's actively being used.*

- **G3 — Time services based on context.** Time when to act or interrupt based on the user's current task and environment.
- **G4 — Show contextually relevant information.** Display information relevant to the user's current task and environment.
- **G5 — Match relevant social norms.** Ensure the experience is delivered in a way users would expect.
- **G6 — Mitigate social biases.** Ensure the AI system's language and behaviors do not reinforce stereotypes.

## When Wrong · G7–G9 {.smaller}

*Invoking, dismissing, and correcting the AI's services.*

**G7 — Support efficient invocation**
Make it easy to invoke or request the AI system's services when needed.

**G8 — Support efficient dismissal**
Make it easy to dismiss or ignore undesired AI system services.

**G9 — Support efficient correction**
Make it easy to edit, refine, or recover when the AI system is wrong.

## When Wrong · G10–G11

*Handling uncertainty gracefully, and explaining after the fact.*

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-field}
**G10 — Scope services when in doubt**

Engage in disambiguation or gracefully degrade the AI system's services when uncertain about a user's goals.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.tag-field}
**G11 — Make clear why the system did what it did**

Enable the user to access an explanation of why the AI system behaved as it did.
:::
:::
:::

## Over Time · G12–G18 {.smaller}

*Feedback, consequences, control, and change management.*

| | |
|---|---|
| **G12** Remember recent interactions | Maintain short term memory and allow efficient reference to it. |
| **G13** Learn from user behavior | Personalize the experience by learning from actions over time. |
| **G14** Update and adapt cautiously | Limit disruptive changes when adapting AI behavior. |
| **G15** Encourage granular feedback | Enable preference feedback during regular interaction. |
| **G16** Convey consequences of actions | Immediately convey how actions impact future AI behavior. |
| **G17** Provide global controls | Allow global customization of what the system monitors. |
| **G18** Notify users about changes | Inform users when capabilities are added or updated. |

## Which Guidelines Apply to Conversational AI? {background-color="#003B5C"}

::: {.kicker}
PART THREE
:::

*Recall Week 5: a conversational interface has no screen. Not every guideline transfers cleanly.*

## Conversational AI's Special Constraint

*The guidelines were built and tested mostly on products with screens.*

::: {.callout}
Amershi et al. tested their 18 guidelines against 20 real products — and found that voice assistants had the largest number of "does not apply" responses of any product category tested. Some guidelines do not directly apply to AI systems that lack a graphical interface.
:::

**Why this matters for your project:** this isn't a flaw in the guidelines — it's a reminder that a validated framework still needs to be applied thoughtfully to a new context.

## Guidelines That Map Directly

*These transfer to voice and chat almost without modification.*

- **G1 — What can it do?** A voice assistant's onboarding can state its scope out loud.
- **G7 / G8 — Invoke & dismiss.** A wake word and "never mind" are natural spoken equivalents of a button.
- **G9 — Correction.** "Actually, cancel that" is a conversational correction move users already know.
- **G12 — Recent memory.** "What did I just ask?" works because dialogue already has a natural sequence.

## Guidelines That Struggle Without a Screen {background-color="#7A0A22"}

*These need real redesign, not just a spoken translation.*

- **G4 — Show contextually relevant information.** "Show" assumes a screen. A voice-only agent must decide what's worth saying aloud.
- **G17 — Provide global controls.** There's no settings menu to point to in a pure voice interface.
- **G11 — Explain why.** Reading a full explanation aloud is slow and easy to forget — even harder to implement well in audio.

## A Worked Example: Applying the Guidelines to a Voice Assistant

*Picking three guidelines and sketching what "applied" actually looks like.*

**G2 · Set expectations of quality**
*"I'm still learning — I might mishear you sometimes, so feel free to repeat yourself."*

**G9 · Support efficient correction**
*A brief pause after every action lets the user say "undo" or "no, I meant…" before the assistant fully commits.*

**G16 · Convey consequences of actions**
*"Got it — I'll remind you at 7 AM, and I won't suggest earlier alarms again unless you ask."*

## Connecting Back: Guidelines Meet the Challenges {background-color="#F19C49"}

*Every guideline exists because of one of Part 1's four challenges.*

| Challenge | Related guidelines |
|---|---|
| **Opacity** | G11 (explain why), G1–G2 (set expectations) |
| **Miscalibrated trust** | G2 (quality expectations), G16 (consequences), G9 (correction) |
| **Brittleness** | G14 (update cautiously), G10 (scope when in doubt) |
| **Explainability** | G11 (explain why), G4 (contextual relevance) |

## Discussion Questions {background-color="#003B5C" .smaller}

*Bring your answers to at least one of these to class.*

1. Pick an AI product you use. Identify one guideline it clearly violates. Using Yang et al.'s framework, is the root cause capability uncertainty, output complexity, or both?
2. Amershi et al. found Guideline 11 (explain why) was relevant but rarely well-implemented. Design a one-sentence spoken explanation your course project's assistant could give for a recommendation.
3. Lee & See describe overtrust and distrust as opposite failure modes. Which guideline(s) most directly protect against each one?
4. Not every one of the 18 guidelines fits a voice-only interface cleanly. Propose a conversational redesign for G17 that doesn't require a settings screen.

## Key Takeaways

*Naming the problem precisely is what makes the guidelines useful, not decorative.*

- AI is difficult to design for two structural reasons — capability uncertainty and output complexity — not because designers lack skill.
- Microsoft's 18 guidelines aren't opinion. They were distilled from 150+ recommendations, tested on 20 real products by 49 practitioners, and refined through four rounds of evaluation.
- The guidelines cluster around four moments: setting expectations initially, behaving well during interaction, handling being wrong gracefully, and building a relationship over time.
- Guidelines built around screens don't all transfer cleanly to conversational AI — a genuine, unresolved design challenge for your own project.

## References {.smaller}

- Yang, Q., Steinfeld, A., Rosé, C., & Zimmerman, J. (2020). Re-examining Whether, Why, and How Human-AI Interaction Is Uniquely Difficult to Design. *CHI '20*, 1–13.
- Amershi, S., Weld, D., Vorvoreanu, M., Fourney, A., Nushi, B., Collisson, P., Suh, J., Iqbal, S., Bennett, P. N., Inkpen, K., Teevan, J., Kikin-Gil, R., & Horvitz, E. (2019). Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction. *CHI '19*, 1–13.
- Lee, J. D., & See, K. A. (2004). Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance. *Human Factors*, 46(1), 50–80.
- Luger, E., & Sellen, A. (2016). "Like Having a Really Bad PA": The Gulf between User Expectation and Experience of Conversational Agents. *CHI '16*, 5286–5297.
- Norman, D. A. (1988). *The Design of Everyday Things.* Basic Books.
